#4744. What is Gonzo? We asked three biologists.

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 13, 2026 9:39 AM EST

Many of the Muppets are pretty easy to pin down, species-wise. Kermit is a frog. Fozzie is a bear. Miss Piggy is, obviously, a feisty piggy. But Gonzo—with his blue-ish fur, bulging eyes, tuft of purple feathers, and long, curved nose that looks a little like a beak—is something of an enigma. The writers of the Muppets have avoided the question of what Gonzo is for years.

Well, in a new episode of Popular Science’s Ask Us Anything podcast, we asked three biologists to break down exactly what Gonzo is. We also talk to Muppets legend and Gonzo performer Dave Goelz to get his take.

Ask Us Anything answers your most outlandish, mind-burning questions—from the everyday things you’ve always wondered to the bizarre things you never thought to ask. So, yes, there’s a reason candy tastes different now and no, you don’t need to worry about Yellowstone’s supervolcano blowing up anytime soon. If you have a question for us, send us a note. Nothing is too silly or simple.

This episode is based on the Popular Science article “What kind of animal is Gonzo?”

Listen and follow Ask Us Anything on your favorite podcast platform:

Spotify | Apple Podcasts | YouTube | Or wherever you get your podcasts.

Sarah Durn: Picture some of the most recognizable characters from The Muppets. Maybe you’re thinking of Kermit the Frog, or Miss Piggy, or Fozzie Bear. But today, we’re talking about a Muppet who’s a little harder to describe: Gonzo. You know the one. He’s got bluish fur, big bulging eyes, a tuft of purple feathers on his head, and a long curved nose that looks a little like a beak.

You might know him as The Great Gonzo, the fearless daredevil, performance artist, and stunt Muppet who eats tires, catches cannonballs bare-handed, and courts his beloved Camilla, who is a chicken. So yeah, Gonzo is a pretty unusual guy. But here’s something you might never have stopped to think about. What exactly is Gonzo?

Is he a bird, a lizard, an alien? All of the above? For decades, Muppets cast and creators have mostly dodged the question when asked, but here at Popular Science, we wanted a more scientific answer. So we asked three biologists to take a closer look at Gonzo’s anatomy and tell us what kind of creature he might be.

Their answers took us somewhere we definitely weren’t expecting, all the way back to the age of the dinosaurs. So what is Gonzo, and can science finally solve one of the Muppets’ greatest mysteries?

Welcome to Ask Us Anything from the editors of Popular Science, where we answer your questions about our weird world. From “does candy taste different now?” to “how do airplane toilets work?” No question is too simple or too out there. I’m Sarah Durn, an editor at Popular Science.

Annie Colbert: And hello, I am Popular Science editor-in-chief and huge Muppets fan, Annie Colbert

SD: Here at PopSci, we’re always pondering weirdo questions.

AC: And this week we’re wondering: What animal might Gonzo be? Is he an animal at all?

SD: It’s a very fair question, one the writers of the Muppets have spent over 50 years dodging. In one film, Gonzo even asked to be called a whatever.

AC: Which is pretty classic Gonzo, but as science journalists, “whatever” doesn’t quite hold up under peer review.

SD: Not at all. So we took Gonzo’s anatomy to actual evolutionary biologists and paleontologists to see if they could decode his unique physiology.

AC: Let me guess. They told you he’s just a funny-looking bird?

SD: That’s what you might think. He’s got that down curved beak thing, a floof atop on his head that kinda looks like feathers, and a chicken for a girlfriend.

But when you look at the clues, like his three unfused fingers and fuzzy skin, things get way weirder.

AC: Weirder than a blue guy who eats rubber tires and catches cannonballs?

SD: Well, at least on a similar level of weird, I guess. Some scientists think his traits point tens of millions of years into the past, past modern birds, straight into the age of carnivorous dinosaurs.

AC: Wait, are you telling me that Gonzo might be closer to a T-Rex than a turkey?

SD: Let’s just say Jurassic Park might need a Muppets section.

AC: Hmm. Now, before we try to decode the Muppet fossil record, we wanna know, what questions are nagging you? If there’s something you’ve always wanted to know, submit your questions by clicking the Ask Us link at popsci.com/ask.

Again, that’s popsci.com/ask, and click the Ask Us link.

AC: We’ll be right back after this quick break to find out if science can really classify the greatest daredevil in puppet history.

SD: And stick around to the end, because we’ll be joined by the legendary David Goelz, the original and longtime performer of Gonzo, to hear his take on what sort of life form Gonzo might be.

And we’re back. Now, Annie, before we dive into the mysteries of Muppet evolution, we need to establish your credentials here a bit, because you are far from just a casual fan. You are a certified Muppet expert.

SD: Okay, so how did your Muppet obsession begin?

AC: You know, there’s no start to my love of Muppets.

I grew up in a Muppet house with The Muppet Show and Sesame Street always on. I’ve always identified as a bit of a whimsical weirdo. I dressed up even as Grundgetta, who is Oscar the Grouch’s girlfriend, for Halloween in fourth grade. No one knew who I was, but I will share a photo, so you can judge for yourselves, listeners.

And I would say generally if people know one or two things about me, it’s either that I have strange cats or that I love the Muppets. It’s a very big part of who I am.

SD: I mean, you have your own Muppet wiki page.

AC: I do! It just appeared one day after I did some fun work with Sesame Street, but it is a life highlight to have.

SD: I mean, so casual, so cool. Um, honestly, I think I’m a little intimidated because I am walking into this episode possessing maybe 1% of your Muppet knowledge. I think I saw a couple of the Muppet films when I was growing up.

AC: Don’t worry at all. The Muppets accept all, even the uninitiated.

SD: Well, I’m very happy to be here as an uninitiated Muppet fan, especially because this episode is just so fun and goofy and feels very PopSci.

AC: Yes, absolutely. I love giving scientific thought to some seriously silly questions because, as we know, science is fueled by curiosity.

SD: Of course. All right, so as our Muppet expert, I have to ask, if you had to put a label on Gonzo, what is he?

AC: Hmm. I think I would probably refer back to Muppet canon and say a whatever.

AC: Right. Well, in the 1981 film The Great Muppet Caper, a few of the Muppets get shipped to London in labeled crates. So Kermit’s says “frog,” Fozzie’s says “bear,” and Gonzo’s just says “whatever.”

AC: Very. But the Muppets haven’t always been super consistent with how they define what Gonzo is.

Three years earlier in the 1979 Muppet Movie, Kermit calls Gonzo sort of like a turkey. And then in 1999 in Muppets From Space, Gonzo was briefly labeled as an extraterrestrial.

AC: But for the most part, his species is left pretty ambiguous. It’s kind of become a running joke.

I may not have your Muppet know-how, but I can definitely ask experts some silly Muppet-related questions.

SD: So the first expert we consulted is Darren Naish, a paleontologist who studies extinct vertebrae anatomy, and Naish lines up a bit with Kermit’s turkey theory. He thinks Gonzo is a bird.

AC: A bird? So is he agreeing with Kermit’s turkey comment?

SD: Sort of. He looked at the evidence. Gonzo is fuzzy, so he’s likely warm-blooded. He’s got four limbs, a backbone, no teeth, and that curved beak-looking snout. And if you add all of those together, Naish says he can’t be anything other than a bird.

AC: Okay. I hear the logic, but I’m not fully abandoning my whatever theory just yet.

SD: Fair enough. Well, Naish actually got way more specific than a turkey. He looks at Gonzo’s slender, down-curving snout and sees an ibis, one of those long-billed wading birds.

AC: Okay, but ibises fly, and Gonzo only flies if he’s shot out of a cannon.

SD: Naish actually thought of that. It turns out birds lose flight all the time in evolutionary history. In fact, an extinct Jamaican ibis from about 10,000 years ago lost the ability to fly, and its wing bones actually evolved into heavy club-like weapons that it used to smack rivals in fights.

AC: Cool. They’re just swinging club hands in a brawl.

AC: I mean, honestly, that sounds extremely Gonzo. But not in a violent way. It’d be in a silly way. He’d be like-

SD: Of course, of course. So Naish’s theory is that Gonzo could be a highly derived flightless ibis.

AC: Okay. I kinda love that, but it still feels a little too normal for him.

SD: Well, hold onto your tuft of blue fuzz. Enter our second paleontologist, Thomas Holtz from the University of Maryland, who specializes in carnivorous dinosaurs. And Holtz looked at Gonzo and said, “You’re looking at the wrong geological era. Gonzo is actually way older, Jurassic kind of old.”

SD: A dinosaur. Holtz looked at Gonzo’s hands, and if you look at modern birds, their wing bones are fused together with drastically reduced digits. But Gonzo, Gonzo has three distinct, fully functioning, unfused fingers on each hand.

AC: True. I mean, he does have to hold his stunt props somehow.

SD: Exactly. And Holtz noted that Gonzo’s body is covered in simple down-like fuzz, with just a few complex feathers on his head. According to Holtz, you only see those two specific traits together, three free fingers and simple fuzzy coats, in early carnivorous dinosaurs from a group called Tetanurae.

AC: Tetanurae? What? Okay, who else is in that club?

SD: Oh, just the ancestors of raptors and early tyrannosaurs.

AC: No way. Tyrannosaurus rex? Is Gonzo related to a T-rex?

SD: Maybe. Holtz points out that other Muppets who are clearly birds, like Big Bird or Camilla and her chicken friends, have modern veined feathers and hard, shiny keratin beaks.

Gonzo has neither. So Holtz argues that if Gonzo is in the bird lineage, he split off tens of millions of years before modern feathers or fused wings ever evolved. He’s a living prehistoric relic.

AC: I don’t think Camilla realizes she’s dating an ancient theropod dinosaur, but you know what, honestly, good for her.

SD: Aim high, Camilla. But we had one more scientist weigh in, Michel Milinkovitch, an evolutionary developmental biologist at the University of Geneva, and he said the whole debate hinges on one single question: What is that tuft on Gonzo’s head made of?

SD: Yes. Milinkovitch says it could just be convergent evolution, a mammal that independently evolved a beak-like snout, like the platypus.

AC: My brain is malfunctioning. So he’s either a modified ibis, a fuzzy Jurassic carnivore, or a bizarre egg-laying mammal cousin.

SD: Yes. You got it. Your brain is doing fine.

SD: And to make matters even more confusing, though, Holtz points out the biggest scientific problem of all: Gonzo’s nose isn’t actually a beak at all.

SD: In birds and turtles, the beak is the mouth. It’s the actual jaw bone covered in hard keratin. But for Gonzo, that big purple nose thing is an extension sitting above and in front of his mouth. It doesn’t have the hard shine of keratin, and it doesn’t move like an elephant’s trunk. Holtz says it’s an anatomical structure that is basically unheard of in vertebrate biology.

AC: Leave it to Gonzo to have a face that literally defies anatomy. My whatever theory still holds water.

SD: It really does. And Darren Naish actually had a great philosophical take on this. He pointed out that nobody asks what creature other Muppets like Animal or Elmo are because they don’t have distinct anatomical clues. But Gonzo has just enough real anatomy, feathers, a beak, three fingers, a chicken for a partner, to make our human brains desperate to categorize him. As Naish put it, “Specificity invites scrutiny.”

AC: And the more details you give us, the more obsessed we become with solving the puzzle.

SD: Exactly. So whether he’s an ibis, a dinosaur, or an evolutionary wild card, science still can’t give us a tidy one-word label.

AC: Truly a dream come true. That’s right after this quick break.

DG: Well, I can answer from our particular corner of the field.

When the Muppets started out, they tended to be almost always abstract characters. There was one humanoid in their first series. The series was called Sam and Friends, and Sam looked like a, a person, but everybody else on the show looked like things we’d never seen before. And then when we went on Sesame Street, this is before, before I was there, actually, they went on Sesame Street, they, it stayed with abstract characters, Ernie and Bert, Grover.

Grover is considered a monster. And they stayed with those abstract characters for quite a long time, and then when we did The Muppet Show, all of a sudden we were surprised to see pigs and chickens…

DG: I remember thinking, “This is weird, the Muppets are abstract. Why do we, why do we have a pig?” You know? “Why do, why do we have a chicken?” It was just an interesting transition ’cause that’s when we went more literal with, with species. Getting around to answering your question, I don’t know what Gonzo is. I have no idea. He was something that Jim built for a previous special, as you know, and when it came time to do The Muppet Show, Jim asked me to do this character who was kind of a loser outsider who does stupid acts and thinks they’re high art.

And then he asked for them to pull Gonzo out. Or that, that puppet that wasn’t Gonzo yet.

AC: What were your first impressions when you saw the puppet itself?

DG: Well, I had seen it before, so it wasn’t a surprise, but it was this pathetic-looking little guy, who had very downcast eyes. He was sort of limited, but I just started making a character out of him, and what my interest in him has always been is his character. And iin that one character, I found that it mirrored me. The reason that it did was because Jerry Juhl, who was our head writer and a very wise person and very funny and mischievous person, could see, I guess, that I was new.

I had no business in show business. I had no training. I had no acting training. We just started The Muppet Show, and Jim tossed me in, and I felt very out of place. I just go, “I don’t belong here. What am I doing in this room?” And so Jerry Juhl helped write Gonzo to be appropriate to where I was in life, and that was phase one. He was an outsider. He had a little bit of a baby talk accent…

DG: like a true newbie. And then as time went by, and I’m talking about years, I got more confident, and then one of our writers, Bill Prady, he started writing Gonzo as being very upbeat and enthusiastic. Like, “That is so cool,” you know, and, and just up for anything, and that became phase two of his character, which coincided with me being more comfortable in my new world And then phase three came when Jerry Juhl wanted to include Dickensian prose in the Muppet Christmas Carol film.

He needed that narrative prose in there, but didn’t want to have a narrator, and he had the idea, because we were very close friends, and he’d watched me go through therapy, and he’d watched me deepen and soften and evolve. He had the idea of letting Gonzo speak those lines.

AC: I feel like people have been asking this question since we all met Gonzo. Why do you think people care so much?

DG: Oh, I think I’ve learned a lot about that in the last, I don’t know, 10 years, let’s say. Whenever I appear at a museum or introduce a screening, people come up to me, and so many people come up and say, “Thank you. Gonzo gave me permission to be different.”

DG: He legitimized it. He made it cool. And a lot of these people are on the spectrum, and they are lovely people who have a hard time in life. And it was unintentional on my part. I didn’t know that they were, that Gonzo was having this effect on people, but he did.

And then about four months ago, I, I realized suddenly that, oh, wait a minute, no, no, this was unconscious on my part. I knew I was different. I didn’t belong in show business. I should be on my parents’ couch, you know, watching on the other end.

AC: Yeah, I feel like, I’m sure people have said this to you, you know, I think people think of Kermit as the heart of the Muppets, and they think of Gonzo as kind of the soul of the Muppets, and I think that nebulousness around what he is, of like not really knowing, I think it allows a lot of people, you know, myself included, that you can find a piece of yourself in him.

If you’ve ever felt excluded or weird, because he is not defined, there is lots of room to sort of hold a piece of him as a fan.

DG: Oh, Annie, that’s absolutely true. Absolutely true. He’s been that for people, and I have to say also that the Muppets as a whole are like that, too. They function the same way.

DG: Jim was a lover of characters. He hired characters. He hired all sorts of unusual people and found something for them to do and let them shine. It’s like I didn’t create Gonzo. It was me and the writers and Jim and the workshop. And these qualities exist in every single character, and there’s somebody out there who responds to every single one.

AC: You have a little bit of like an engineering and design background, right?

DG: I do, yeah. I was an industrial designer by training.

AC: Yeah, and I think especially lately there’s this sort of stark line between art and science, but you know, what we see, especially at Popular Science, is we see really amazing innovations can happen when art and science overlap.

So how do you bring a little bit of that engineering mind to playing a Muppet?

DG: A couple of things. First of all, when I first began, I already knew how to build puppets because I was trained as a designer at Art Center College of Design, and the design process was something that my dad inculcated into me, and then ArtCenter set in place.

And the design process that I use is about defining the problem, whether it’s a character, a performance, a glasses case, a typewriter. Whatever it is, it’s very important to know what the problem is, and it’s not always obvious. Listen, the reason I love that approach is that the more you hone in on the problem, the clearer the solution becomes.

AC: One final question. Because we’re Popular Science, I must ask about the Muppets’ preeminent scientist, Dr. Bunsen Honeydew-

AC: whom, of course, you also perform. If Bunsen, or Dr. Honeydew, he earned his degree, won a Nobel Prize, what do you think it would be for?

DG: Well, first of all, the idea is preposterous-

DG: On its face. That’s a great question. If he won a Noble Prize, what would it be for? A Nobel Peace Prize. All he’s done in life is make stupid inventions and hurt his assistant.

DG: So it really is a preposterous notion. I can’t even answer it.

I can’t. It’s just a mind-boggling question. I don’t have any idea how he could possibly be recognized for anything. I will tell you this, that Bunsen was, Bunsen was derived from a lot of scientists that I knew when I was in Silicon Valley. It wasn’t anybody directly, but it was this whole idea of being focused on electrons and being focused on tiny, tiny, very specific things, and losing the big picture.

DG: Yeah. ‘Cause it’s interesting you know, a scientist might be way deep into making a laser interferometer, and the science of it would be so riveting. And then my job was to come along and say, “Okay, what does it look like? How do you use it?” So I was, like, the user end of this whole deal. And, and so as a generalist, I could view the science world and the engineering world, and, uh, poke a little fun at it.

AC: Absolutely. Science is fun. We like to remind people.

AC: I will take off my journalist hat just for a second and say thank you so much for doing the podcast, but also just thank you so much for Gonzo. What you said about people who have maybe been called different or weird, it definitely resonates with me.

I’ve loved the Muppets my entire life, and being called weird my whole life is such a compliment because there’s so much joy and whimsy in the weirdos of Muppets, and Gonzo is such the epitome of that, that I thank you so much, Dave, for joining us today.

SD: Oh my gosh, was your inner Muppet heart exploding while talking to Dave? Yes. He seemed so wonderful.

AC: Yeah, he is just an absolute gem of a human. I did not even try to keep my fandom in check ’cause he’s a legend, and he’s genuinely meant so much to me as a Muppet fan.

SD: He’s the best. Oh my God. So after hearing from Dave and all of our biologists where do you, Muppet expert, officially land on the taxonomy of a Gonzo?

AC: Okay, I started the episode firmly on team whatever, but now I kinda love the idea that Camilla is casually dating a prehistoric dinosaur. But I also like the idea that Gonzo doesn’t have to be defined. He can be something different for everyone, like, whatever they need him to be.

SD: But the dinosaur theory does make his cannonball catching stunt seem a lot more on brand for a T-Rex relative.

And if you like our show, leave a rating and a review.

SD: Which Muppet do you want scientists to analyze next? Tell us in the comments. Please. Our producer is Alan Haburchak. This week’s episode was based on an article written for Popular Science by Niranjana Rajalakshmi, and a massive thank you to the legendary Dave Goelz for joining us.

AC: Thank you, team. Thank you, Dave, and thanks all you Muppets for listening.

SD: And one more time, if you want something you’ve always wondered about explained on a future episode, go to popsci.com/ask and click the Ask Us link. Until next time, stay weird wherever you are, and keep the questions coming.

#4743. BYD’s full-size luxury SUV has a wheel problem, and it’s fixing it for free

BYD is apologizing after a supplier error left some owners of its new full-size flagship SUV with the wrong wheels.

The Great Tang, or Da Tang as it’s called in China, is the first flagship D-segment SUV under its Dynasty series, the largest and most luxurious SUV from the lineup.

After opening preorders at the Beijing Auto Show in April, BYD said the high-end SUV secured over 30,000 preorders in 24 hours. Two weeks later, preorders reached over 100,000.

By the time it went on sale in mid-June, over 150,000 buyers had preordered the Great Tang, marking a new record for a single BYD model.

While it has been the top-selling pure electric large SUV for two months, with more than 10,000 sold since it hit the market, BYD issued an apology on November 11 for fitting the wrong front and rear wheel rims on some Great Tang models.

The apology comes after several owners complained that the wheels were improperly installed on their vehicles.

BYD said the issue stemmed from a coding error by the wheel mesh assembly supplier, which led to incorrect assembly on some Great Tang vehicles.

The company said it “immediately” launched an investigation and corrected the issue so newly built vehicles will not be affected. In addition, the supplier introduced a new visual error-prevention mechanism to limit issues like this going forward.

BYD said the issue does not affect the vehicle’s handling or pose a safety risk during driving.

The company said owners can take affected vehicles to their local service center for a free inspection and professional wheel rim replacement. It’s also offering a replacement vehicle or compensation for transportation expenses.

Effective immediately, BYD said, the warranty on affected Great Tang vehicles will also be restarted.

The Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest Premium EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500).

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries. While the base Premium model uses a 105.79 kWh battery, the Flagship EV trim uses a larger 130.15 kWh battery that delivers up to 590 miles (950 km) of CLTC range. It starts at 269,900 yuan ($40,000).

The Great Tang is huge, measuring 5,263 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,800 mm high, with a wheelbase of 3,130 mm.

In comparison, that’s bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 and Kia EV9. It’s closer in size to the Li Auto L9.

Based on a 1,000V architecture with BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the electric SUV can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

After launching in China, BYD executive vice president Stella Li said the flagship SUV will go on sale in Europe and other overseas markets by the end of 2026 or early 2027.

#4742. What a Trillion Dollar Industry Cannot Give You

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

Two thousand years ago, the Tamil poet Avvaiyar wrote a line that every child in Tamil Nadu still learns: Arithu, arithu, maanidaraai pirathal arithu. Rare, rare it is to be born human. And then she went further. Rarer still, she said, to be born whole, without the body failing you from the start.

I think about that verse every November, and this year more than most.

In the past month, our team published a randomized pilot trial of yogic breathing and meditation for adults with long COVID, and a study in people living with Parkinson's disease. When you sit with these patients, the suffering is not abstract. A woman in the long COVID trial told our interviewers she had developed “a mental block about breathing because of all the breathing problems.”

Think about what it means to be afraid of your own breath.

What we offered them was modest: a few minutes of breathing practice and a guided meditation, taught online, done at home. We did not cure anyone. The data showed that breathlessness eased by a clinically meaningful margin, fatigue and mood improved, and nobody was harmed. Temporary relief. Less anxiety. A way to live more comfortably with a condition that isn't going away.

And when you see them at one level, you feel something else, which is harder to say out loud. You feel fortunate. You were born, for now at least, without that burden. You have been handed the capacity to experience this life in its full depth, and most days, you forget to use it.

I am a physician scientist, so let me be precise about what we know. Across the published studies from our center, the measures move in one direction. Miracle of Mind, a single seven-minute guided meditation, shifted self-rated affect in 1,325 people, with the largest shifts in those who started lowest. High-density EEG in 103 people showed brain rhythms begin to reorganize within two to three minutes of the same practice and peak around seven. Long-term practitioners carry brains that read about six years younger than their chronological age on sleep EEG. And in the long COVID trial, three weeks of practice moved breathlessness, fatigue, and mood against a waitlist control.

None of this is mystical. It is what happens to attention, emotion, and physiology when a person turns inward in a structured way. Meditation has a distinct origin and an enormous body of technical work from India, and it belongs to everyone, East or West. At its core, it raises awareness. And raising awareness is the most reliable tool I know for the stress and anxiety that come with simply being alive right now.

We are living through the construction of a trillion-dollar artificial intelligence industry. These systems solve mathematical problems that defeat most of us, and they connect islands of knowledge in ways no single human mind can. They matter. They will make medicine safer, work easier, and life more comfortable, and I use them every day.

What this industry has really done is put very strong technology into the hands of the common person. A capability that belonged to institutions a few years ago now sits in a teenager's pocket. Some of us may even be over-equipped, holding more power than our habits are prepared for. It is a knife with two edges. At one end, it accelerates learning in ways that would have seemed miraculous to my teachers. At the other, it can be misused, carelessly or deliberately, at a scale we have not seen before.

That makes this the moment to hold the instrument with precise awareness. No regulator, and no model, can do that for the person holding it. It is left to us. And that is why raising individual awareness and individual consciousness is not a spiritual luxury alongside the technology. It is the one investment that keeps pace with it.

But the machines are not going to give us the human experience. The profoundness we are seeking does not arrive through an interface. It has to come from within. There is no evidence that these systems have such experiences themselves, and we do not know how we would tell if they did. What they can give is comfort. What they cannot give is the goosebumps.

Consider basketball. Analytics tell every team to shoot the three, and on average, the teams that listen win more regular season games. Then the playoffs arrive, and something else takes over. Composure. Fear. The ability to stay present when the arithmetic says you should already have lost. Teams built on the average falter there, because the average was never the game. The same is true of art, of music, of the moment a surgeon's hands know something before the mind does. The human experience is where greatness lives, and it is not a calculation.

The yogic tradition described the mind with a precision we are only now catching up to. It named 16 parts in four categories: buddhi, the intellect that dissects and decides; ahankara, the sense of identity that tells the intellect whose side it is on; manas, the vast silo of memory, running back through evolution; and chitta, pure intelligence, unsullied by memory, the dimension that is simply aware.

A machine can be built to imitate the first three. It can reason, be given a persona, and hold more memory than any of us. Chitta is a different matter. That is the intelligence no one can touch, and it is the ground on which every meditation practice stands.

The same tradition that mapped the mind also told us how to live in it, and the instructions are more practical than people expect.

Sadhguru, my spiritual master, says: Be a mother to the whole world. That is not sentiment. It is a standard. Absolute inclusion, absolute compassion, extended without first checking whether the other person deserves it. No algorithm optimizes for that, because it is not an outcome. It is a way of being.

Then there is acceptance, which is widely misread as passivity. Consider your work. You may or may not get the promotion you seek or the position you have earned. You have only two choices. Stay, and keep raising your capability until the question answers itself. Or step back, look at the whole picture, and if the picture says so, leave. Both are acceptance. What acceptance rules out is the third option most of us choose: staying and resenting it.

And there is agency. Sadhguru says, every action you take is yours. Every reaction, too. The moment you accept that, you stop waiting for the world to arrange itself before you can be well, and you become, in the most literal sense, the author of your own experience.

Inclusion, acceptance, agency. These are enormous pieces of intelligence, worked out over millennia by people who had no instruments beyond their own attention. The machines can remind us of them. They cannot practice them for us. That part, like the goosebumps, is ours.

So, this Thanksgiving, I am grateful for the things my instruments can measure, and more grateful for the things they cannot. I am grateful to have been born human, and whole enough to sit on a cushion and close my eyes. I am grateful for the patients who do the practice anyway, breath by careful breath. And I am grateful for a tradition that asks me to be a mother to the whole world and gives me the tools to try. Above all, I am grateful for the goosebumps that arrive, unbidden, in nearly every meditation, the surest evidence I have that something here no industry will replicate.

If you have seven minutes this week, spend them with your eyes closed doing the Miracle of Mind. The machines will still be there when you open them. So, I hope you will.

#4741. Grad student finds New Mexico’s first Canada lynx in 25 years

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 13, 2026 11:00 AM EST

In June, New Mexico State University graduate student William Grooms was using motion-sensing cameras to investigate wildlife in Carson National Forest in northern New Mexico. And when he looked through his first images, he spotted something flabbergasting.

His cameras had captured a series of photographs of a Canada lynx (Lynx canadensis)—a wild cat that hasn’t been documented in the state for around 25 years. But Grooms had to make sure it wasn’t actually a bobcat (Lynx rufus), which is a similar-looking species.

“It caught my eye because the cat in the image had the characteristic ear tufts and facial ruff [of bobcats], but it was lacking the black spots that are typical of bobcats,” Grooms, who is studying in the department of Fish, Wildlife and Conservation Ecology, tells Popular Science. “We also have a good image of the tail, which on lynx has a solid black tip compared to a bobcat whose tail has white on the underside, so my confidence grew.”

He and his team also showed the image to other researchers for confirmation. Ultimately, there’s no doubt about the fact that the big cat slinking through the dark was indeed a Canada lynx. The species lives in dense boreal and subalpine forests and woodlands throughout much of Canada and Alaska. They have long legs, grayish or yellowish-brown coats, and wide fur-lined paws.

Their main prey are snowshoe hares (Lepus americanus), which they follow into the forest understory—the ground-level area of downed trees and dense vegetation beneath which the hares hide and live. The problem is that these kinds of habitats are fire hazards. Recent forest fire mitigation efforts include decreasing dangerous fuel loads via thinning, prescribed burning, or timber harvesting.

“While these tactics reduce the risk of severe fires, they also remove important habitat features,” Grooms explains. “Our objective is to provide managers with practical, science-based advice regarding what effects fuel reduction treatments and timber harvesting have on wildlife in the Southern Rocky Mountains so that they can make well-informed decisions as they go about their task of managing our nation’s forests.”

Simply knowing that at least one Canada lynx was in the area provides more data for this mission.

#4739. Obesity in Your 20s and 30s May Increase Cancer Risk Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

The risk for cancer became higher as weight increased. The highest rates were seen in those with severe obesity and abdominal obesity.

This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.

Rates of both obesity and early onset cancer are rising among younger adults globally.

This study analyzed data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The researchers identified 6,313,338 adults ages 20 to 39 who had no history of cancer and who underwent standardized national health screenings.

The researchers followed the participants for an average of 11 years.

Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into five groups ranging from underweight to class II obesity using the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for Asian populations. Waist circumference was also measured as an indicator of abdominal adiposity.

During the analysis, the researchers adjusted for various factors such as:

Over the follow-up period, there were 151,893 cases of cancer among the participants. The incidence rate increased progressively based on obesity categories, from 1.84% in “normal-weight” individuals to 2.24% in class I obesity and 2.62% in class II obesity.

The strongest associations were seen in the following cancers:

Obesity was not associated with breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 50.

Ketan Thanki, MD, board certified colorectal surgeon with the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained to Healthline that obesity itself causes states that promote cancer formation.

This current study focused on the Korean population. However, the connection between obesity and cancer risk is a global issue.

Previous research has shown that around 10% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States are associated with obesity. Obesity also accounts for up to 50% of certain cancers, including endometrial and liver cancer.

The study also showed that waist circumference, which indicates abdominal obesity, may be linked to cancer risk that is similar to that of individuals with overweight.

The study researchers used the thresholds set out by the Korean Society for the Study of Obesity. These thresholds put the waist circumference cutoff at over 90 cm (35.4 in) for males and over 85cm (33.46 in) for females.

These are not universal cutoffs. According to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), waist circumference measurements that can increase your risk of negative health issues are 101.6 cm (40 in) for males and 88.9 cm (35 in) for females.

Previous research has also suggested an association between waist circumference and cancer risk, independent of BMI. One study showed a potential 11% increased risk of cancer in people with a waist circumference over the thresholds, even if they were physically active.

The current study found that males had a higher relative association between obesity and cancer, while females showed higher absolute risk.

The researchers also found that the absolute risk was higher in adults ages 30 to 39.

Those who currently smoke or who have ever smoked were also found to have a higher risk of developing cancer than those who have never smoked.

“Diet, exercise, and now medications can all be used very effectively to reduce one’s weight and, hopefully as a result, cancer risk,” Thanki said.

He also noted that, due to differences between South Korean populations and those in other countries such as the United States, further studies will be needed to determine how this translates across other populations.

“But I think this trend will likely extend across all cultures,” he said.

#4738. Ghosts don’t scare German shepherds

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 13, 2026 12:00 PM EST

The German shepherd was originally bred to do exactly what their name implies, but a lot has changed since Max von Stephanitz introduced the breed in 1899. Today, the German shepherd is one of the world’s most recognizable and popular dogs, largely due to their intelligence, trainability, and companionship. You’re just as likely to spot one of them at an airport sniffing for contraband as you are at a kennel club competition.

But a good “work” German shepherd and a good show dog require two very different sets of traits. According to researchers at Sweden’s Uppsala University, these specific qualities are so pronounced that they’re even visible at the genetic level. What’s more, many of these genes can also be seen in humans.

“It’s interesting that we can now see that this selective breeding has indeed led to differences between working dogs and show dogs among German shepherds—differences that can be seen at both the behavioral and genetic levels,” Uppsala University genomics researcher Kerstin Lindblad-Toh explained in a recent profile.

Lindblad-Toh and her colleagues laid out their findings in a study recently published in the journal Animal Genetics. To assess the iconic breed, the team reviewed a massive dataset of 23,000 German shepherds who previously participated in a standardized behavioral test known as the Dog Mentality Assessment (DMA). During the DMA, canines are exposed to a range of situations, such as meeting strangers, play time, and even encountering imposing, ghostly figures. The team discovered that while German shepherds often scored higher for traits like neuroticism and shyness, the breed’s working dogs generally exhibited more curiosity, less fear, and a willingness to socialize with people.

“Breeders of working dogs have selected and bred the ones that really enjoy working; it’s a bit like a game for them,” said Lindblad-Toh.

From there, the researchers gathered blood samples and mapped the genomes of 373 German shepherds who previously took the DMA. Some of these behavioral divergences were so stark that the study’s authors could pinpoint them in the dogs’ genetics.

“We could then see that there were areas in the genome where differences could be seen in the dogs depending on how curious or playful they were, for example,” Lindblad-Toh said. “That meant that we were able to identify some of the genes in working dogs that are linked to curiosity and playfulness.”

In some instances, the same genes influencing German shepherd personalities are also tied to the same behaviors in humans. This means it may be possible to further explore human psychology with the aid of our best animal friends. Although Lindblad-Toh cautioned that their study is “just a first step” along this path, they hope to learn more about specific breed genetic traits and their overlap with owners.

“We now have an example of how we might also acquire more knowledge about different behaviors in people with [the] help of dogs in the longterm,” she said.

#4736. The Holidays on a Tight Budget

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

“Although we had no money, I was rich as I could be, in my coat of many colors, my mama made for me.” —Dolly Parton

In the song “Times A-Getting Hard, Boys,” Pete Seeger famously captured the tune from Carl Sandburg’s collection, revised by Lee Hays, referring to the debt-ridden farmers who abandoned their land and migrated to California. It was the Dust Bowl, yet another Depression-era tragedy.

Granted, we are not close to the Great Depression now. But the wealth gap is near historic highs, and for much of the nation, economic hardship is on the front burner, just in time for the holidays.

Bottom line: Families are paying more for just about everything that matters most. So how can we travel, host, and preserve our holiday traditions under this kind of financial stress?

We are all influenced by the idyllic Hallmark portrayal of the holidays on TV and social media. It’s easy to fall prey to ideals of perfection, only to have our expectations dashed by reality.

Let’s face it. Even in great economic times, the holidays are stressful, laced with conflict and inevitable disappointment.

We begin with the adults. As the flight attendant says, “If the cabin pressure drops, put your own oxygen mask on first, then help the person next to you.” We are better at managing our kids’ stress when we first take care of our own.

Kids don’t worry about money the way adults do, but they feel our stress, and it has an impact on them.

For all of us, adults and kids alike, self-care is essential: eating well, exercising, getting restorative sleep, and making time for meditation or relaxation. In short, finding (free) ways to reduce stress.

Stress due to financial strain is not all that different than stress induced by other psychosocial factors.

But one thing is different. Even in therapy, talking about one’s finances can be rare. Clinicians will hear about all sorts of complex issues, but some research has shown that rarely, if ever, does a patient talk about money—their income, net worth, debt, and attendant issues for the family.

So, how can we have meaningful conversations with our kids and other family members about what we can afford this year?

Tailor the conversation to your child’s age. Remember that younger kids don’t need details about the family budget, but they do need reassurance. School-age kids can understand trade-offs, and they often like being part of the solution. While teens can handle more nuanced conversations about financial matters, they’re also most likely to feel the sting of comparison with peers.

Before we change anything this year, we need to know what our kids, young and old, are thinking.

Gatherings are super important: Coming together does more than we think. A review of 148 studies following more than 308,000 people found that those with stronger social relationships had a 50 percent higher likelihood of surviving over the study’s period than those with weaker ties, and this finding remained consistent across age, sex, and even initial health. Gatherings save lives.

Try these suggestions for keeping the social ties strong despite financial challenges.

Remember that giving is as vital for the giver as the receiver. In a study during the COVID-19 pandemic, 777 people were asked to perform three acts of kindness each week for two weeks. Those assigned to be kind to others experienced significant decreases in depression, anxiety, and loneliness. Here are some ideas to kick around for giving.

These are not easy times. But when we share our hardships, we fare better. Don’t worry alone!

Published Nov 13, 2026 1:09 PM EST

One little bear cub in Southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest is a true model of bravery. The park’s rangers have awarded the unnamed black bear (Ursus americanus) cub with the 2026 Courageous Cub award for persevering when he got himself in a little pickle this summer. The cub belongs to a forgetful mother bear named Dory, who had two cubs this season.

“This little cub of Dory’s went on a big adventure. He got lost, ran down the trail a half mile and approached visitors as if to ask, ‘Are you my mommy?’ Then got scared and ran off in the wrong direction,” the Tongass rangers write. “Hours later he came running back up the trail sniffing out where mama was.”

Black bears like this family have a very keen sense of smell. It is debated just how far away they can smell, but it is at least two miles and could be up to 20. Fortunately, the cub was able to use some of that sniffing power to find both Dory and his other sibling.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States. It covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau, and includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. This makes the creek a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, at least 39 bears feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

#4734. Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: What a Decade of Bedtime Stories Taught Me About Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember. We started with the likes of “Goodnight Batcave” and the lesser-known-in-the-US but oh-so-wonderful collection of verse-driven classics from former UK Children’s Laureate Julia Donaldson.

We moved on to B.J. Novak’s anarchic love letter to the power of words (and to great typography), “The Book With No Pictures.”

We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.

When my eldest, Amelia, hit 6, it was time to roll out the big guns.

Over the last 5 years (she’s now 11), I’ve read the seven Harry Potter books aloud twice, complete with all the voices: once to Amelia on her own, once to both her and her brother, Henry, two years her junior.

I had feared she wouldn’t be keen on another helping, but Amelia immersed herself once more in the world of Hogwarts with no hesitation and took immense joy in watching Henry discover for himself every twist and turn on Harry’s journey.

We have done the same thing with Tolkien’s “The Hobbit” and his fantasy masterpiece “The Lord of the Rings,” and are currently midway through “The Two Towers” on our second go around.

There’s a huge amount of reciprocal joy we take from this nightly ritual, beyond the practical benefits of providing a calming demarcation between the end of the day and the wind-down to sleep.

For me, it comes as either a break in my working day or a signal that it’s over, depending on how hectic things are.

For the kids, it’s an all-too-rare chance to get me all to themselves, no deadlines, screens, or other distractions to pull me away from being anything but 100% present.

For all three of us, it’s a literal (and literary!) warm blanket — a chance to escape under the covers to familiar worlds and familiar faces. It is, in short, incredibly good for our well-being.

And yet, in the world of health information — including on this site — thousands, if not millions, of reading hours are dedicated to the benefits of nutrition, sleep, and exercise as the building blocks of good health. Reading itself rarely makes that shortlist.

For me, it unequivocally deserves a place on it. Research seems to support that case. Even if we need more of it to really understand how and why.

A recent editorial in Psychological Medicine co-authored by Barbara Sahakian, Professor of Clinical Neuropsychology at Cambridge University, draws on a broad range of research linking reading for pleasure to better mental health and greater empathy.

The positive impact of reading on young people — just like Amelia and Henry — also carries evidence.

Among more than 10,000 US adolescents, those who started reading for pleasure early had fewer mental health problems, spent less time on screens and slept more. Although, per an earlier column of mine, I can’t vouch for the sleep side of things when it comes to early bird Henry.

For many, reading can be a form of therapy that improves well-being. Bibliotherapy is a complementary therapeutic tool for emotional release and reduced stress and anxiety, with its roots traced back to ancient civilizations.

There’s even research suggesting a link between a love of reading and a lower risk of cognitive decline.

In a 2003 study of people aged 75 and over, reading was associated with a 35% lower risk of dementia over roughly five years.

A separate 14-year study from 2022 found that people who read at least weekly saw less cognitive decline, whatever their level of education.

A happy (and healthy) by-product of this love of being read to is that both my kids have now started reading to me at bedtime. Henry recently read “Jeffy the Burglar’s Cat” to us, a lesser-known but no less compelling chapter book by Ursula Moray Williams that was a staple of my own childhood. And we’ve enjoyed several books from Amelia, including the wistful tale of friendship and the circle of life, “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White – not a dry eye in the house for the final few chapters of that one.

They’ve also gone off and re-read the Harry Potter books and “The Hobbit” to themselves.

The research above links reading to many health benefits: better attention and memory, fewer mental health problems, more sleep, less time on screens, and greater empathy. I haven’t measured any of those impacts empirically in our house. Nor am I naive to the fact that as they get older, they’ll ultimately grow out of me reading to them, with school, extracurricular activities, their friends, and inevitably screens competing for more and more of their time.

Come what may, though, I know that a child who considers missing a reading session as the most cardinal of cardinal sins, and who scrambles for the chance to read aloud to their dad at bedtime is, at that moment, concentrating, empathizing, discovering and growing.

Researchers are clear that studies espousing the benefits of reading show association rather than proof, and it’s evident that more experimental work and deeper research are needed to ensure the complex cause and effect stands on firm scientific ground.

Regardless, it’s a healthy habit Amelia, Henry and I are very happy to keep, and with a bit of luck, I’ll get to pass it on to their kids one day.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4732. Divers release first footage of SS ‘United States’ after intentional sinking

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 13, 2026 2:00 PM EST

It took a few hours longer than expected, but the SS United States now rests at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico. The nearly 1,000-foot-long ocean liner sank off the coast of Pensacola, Florida, to a depth of about 190 feet on November 11, where it is now officially the world’s largest artificial reef. In the years ahead, biologists and conservationists will monitor the vessel’s remains as numerous marine species slowly convert the ship into their own home.

Ahead of the next phase in the United States’ recycled life, divers from the RV Explorer swam to document the vessel’s location and post-scuttling condition. On November 13, the team released a brief video of their successful excursion. Interestingly, the footage shows the ship is resting upright on the ocean floor despite initially sinking on its side.

“It was just epic,” diver Rustin Cassway told a local Philadelphia news outlet. “It was very cleaned up. I mean, you could see people really took their time to clean it really nicely.”

The project marks the first time ecologists will be able to monitor a shipwreck’s transformation in real-time. Researchers now plan to conduct annual visits to the SS United States to chart not only the artificial reef’s progress, but how the ship’s materials may affect the surrounding ocean conditions.

In its heyday, the SS United States was the world’s fastest ocean liner. Larger than the RMS Titanic, she was the most powerful, advanced, and modern passenger liner when she first took to the ocean in 1952. In addition to the 1,700 passengers, 7,935 quarts of ice cream and 500 pounds of caviar were also on board. During that maiden voyage (July 3-7, 1952), she broke the transatlantic speed record held by the RMS Queen Mary by over 10 hours. The United States made the crossing from the United Kingdom to New York in three days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes at an average speed of 40.96 mph.

She was designed by naval architect William Francis Gibbs (August 24, 1886 – September 6, 1967), and was built to be converted into a troopship if the United States Navy needed during a time of war. But she never was called into military service. Instead, the United States transported immigrants and celebrities, including future President and First Lady John and Jacqueline Kennedy, actors Grace Kelly, Gary Cooper, and Marilyn Monroe, artist Salvador Dali, and musicians Duke Ellington and Irving Berlin. Walt Disney even filmed parts of the 1962 comedy Bon Voyage aboard the ship.

An engineering marvel, some of the key design features were in the rudder, radar mast, and propellers.

The rudder was designed for good maneuverability at high speeds. The Titanic’s relatively small rudder was one factor behind the ship’s collision with an iceberg and tragic sinking in 1912.

The SS United States had the latest radar equipment, which allowed the crew to see the locations of  other ships and objects in the ocean despite the weather. It was among the first ocean liners to use radar, which was located at one of the highest points on the ship, so in addition to her radar “eyes,” a lookout could be stationed there to warn the captain of any danger in the ship’s path.

Considered a top-secret design, the ship had four propellers—two with four blades and two with five. According to the SS United States Conservancy, this configuration was tested and selected for its superior hydrodynamic performance. The propeller design was overseen by a pioneering Gibbs & Cox engineer named Elaine Kaplan.

Ocean liners became a less attractive option once air travel became quicker and less expensive. The SS United States ceased operations in 1969, and stayed in drydock in several cities before becoming the world’s largest artificial reef.

#4731. The Lame Duck: A Leader's Exit Can Be Bad or Good

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

It happens all the time. A leader’s time in the role is coming to an end. A leader who is completing the end of tenure in a top-level leadership position can either do an organization great harm or much good. What happens when a leader is a lame duck, with a known date for terminating their tenure? It all depends on the leader’s intent, their motivation, and how the leader’s team deals with it.

Neglect. What happens when a leader mentally disengages from their position and takes a “who cares” attitude? In one instance, a department director who was finishing his last few months simply stopped leading—communicating much less, canceling meetings that focused on moving the company forward, and not providing much information or feedback to direct reports. The organization came to a virtual standstill that lasted for a while, and it took new, energetic leadership to recover.

Trashing the Place. Even worse, a leader can decide to cause real damage. This can occur when the leader has been fired or feels unfairly treated. The leader might end promising and/or profitable projects. Resources might be rerouted to the leader’s benefit. More subtly, the leader might pit team members against one another and create a toxic work culture.

Motivational Malaise. A leader’s lack of interest and activity as they come to the end of their tenure can be contagious, affecting the motivation of other employees (“If the leader doesn’t seem to care, why should I?” “The leader is taking a lot of personal time off, so I guess it’s OK.”). The leader’s negativity or simple disinterest can be infectious and affect the motivation of others.

Allow Others to Step Up to Leadership. A good leader develops leadership capacity in others. When a leader is exiting, it is important to provide opportunities for direct reports to take on leadership roles and activities. A much-celebrated CEO who was retiring told me that he knew that the organization would be in good hands after his departure because he had worked to develop his successors’ leadership. Delegating responsibility and sharing the leadership is the key to developing followers into leaders.

Strengthen Existing Processes. When a leader’s departure is inevitable, it is a good time for the leader to do a comprehensive evaluation of the organization’s operations. Rather than winding things down, it’s a good time to focus on improvement. What could be working better? What new initiatives should be fast-tracked? Rather than taking it easy, the departing leader should ramp things up.

Leave a Legacy. An effective leader who is in the waning stages of tenure needs to realize that it is important to continue efforts to improve the organization and its operations. This is the legacy that a good leader leaves behind. The departure should be positive, formative, and free from regrets.

#4730. Europe’s electric car sales jump 49% as global EV sales grow

Global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026. But that North American rebound comes with a big catch.

Drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to new data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. That’s down 3% from September, but it brings sales for the first 10 months of 2026 to 17.5 million – up 5% from the same period last year.

Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.

Europe sold 510,000 EVs in October, up 36% year over year. Fully electric cars did most of the work: BEV sales rose 49%, while plug-in hybrids grew 7%.

That puts October’s growth ahead of Europe’s 31% increase for the year so far. The region has now sold 4.5 million EVs in 2026.

Sales fell 17% from September’s record, but September got a boost from the UK’s twice-yearly registration plate change. The year-over-year figures give a clearer view of how quickly the market is growing.

Germany’s EV share topped 45% of new car sales, its highest level since December 2022. That earlier peak came as buyers rushed to get cars before subsidy cuts took effect. Fully electric car sales in Germany rose almost 80% from a year earlier to more than 95,000.

UK EV sales increased 30%. That’s particularly notable because the Electric Car Grant was already available in October 2025, although fewer models qualified then. So this growth comes against a market that was already getting government support.

And in Portugal, EVs accounted for 55% of new car sales in October, following a sharp rise in their market share over the past few months.

North American EV sales rose 24% year over year to 130,000 in October, the region’s first annual increase of 2026. Sales were flat from September, while the year-to-date decline narrowed to 21%, from 24% a month earlier. The region has sold 1.3 million EVs so far this year.

US EV sales reached around 110,000 units in October.

But here’s the catch: October 2025 was the first month after the federal EV tax credit expired. The credit ended for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and sales dropped sharply afterward.

October 2026 is therefore being compared with a month when sales plummeted. A positive annual number doesn’t mean US demand has returned to its pre-expiration level.

“October is the first month compared against a period without the US federal tax credit, and the US market has stabilized at a lower level rather than recovered,” said Charles Lester, Benchmark’s data manager.

The flat month-over-month figure helps tell that story: Sales have steadied, but the market is operating from a lower base.

China sold 1.14 million EVs in October, up 5% from September but down 12% year over year. That annual decline was smaller than September’s 18% drop.

Sales through October reached 9.1 million, down 11%, compared with a 13% year-to-date decline at the end of September.

Even with fewer EVs being sold, their share of China’s new car market reached a fresh high. That’s because the wider passenger car market is shrinking faster.

Chinese automakers are continuing to produce vehicles and look overseas for buyers. Passenger car exports of new energy vehicles – China’s category covering BEVs and PHEVs – reached nearly 600,000 in October. That’s another monthly record, up from 558,000 in September.

Those exports face more pressure ahead. The EU has agreed to cap imports of Chinese-built hybrids, and China will reduce its EV export VAT rebate from 13% to 9% starting April 1, 2027.

Outside China, Europe, and North America, EV sales rose 85% year over year to 300,000 in October. Those markets have bought 2.6 million EVs so far in 2026, up 93%.

Australia’s sales jumped more than 200% in October, and EVs have gained market share sharply this year. But that hasn’t translated into healthy dealer profits, according to Benchmark. More brands, many of them Chinese, are competing for buyers, spreading sales across more companies and squeezing dealer margins.

Brazil’s growth has also been huge, although Benchmark cautions that some of its drivers are temporary. Importers brought vehicles in ahead of phased tariff increases, a fuel crisis pushed more buyers toward EVs, and BYD increased production at its Brazilian factory.

Nothing like consumer economics to drive sales. Local story about consumer economics: Windturbines on land is not popular. However, the locals realised they could heat their home for $300/year (in Denmark(!)) with these wind turbines and then they were tolerated! Same with cars - people gravitate to cheaper alternatives despite the more frequent charging and initial higher prices.

As the tariff increases take full effect and fuel price pressure eases, Benchmark expects those boosts to fade. BYD’s local production, which will also supply Argentina and Mexico, is set to become the main remaining support for that growth.

#4729. Robo-frog swims with liquid crystal muscles powered by light

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 13, 2026 3:00 PM EST

A silicone frog built by engineers at Denmark’s Aarhus University can’t swim nearly as fast as its amphibian inspiration, but it still manages to get the job done without any moving parts. The odd invention owes its slow-but-steady aquatic maneuvering to a set of six artificial muscles specially designed to contract when exposed to near-infrared light.

The team’s novel system is detailed in a study recently published in the journal Advanced Materials Technologies. Although similar setups may one day boost the capabilities of soft robots tasked with search and rescue or environmental monitoring, its creators are a bit more realistic about this frog-bot’s near-term uses.

“I could easily imagine these robots being used as toys before we see them on rescue missions,” Cecilie Ryberg, Aarhus University chemist and study co-author, said in a profile. “I think people would have fun playing with a frog like this using a suitable light source.”

Each of the robot’s muscles is built using crystal elastomers. These materials are specifically manufactured to contract while they are heating, and then revert back to their original shape once cooled. In this case, Ryberg and her collaborators also added a molecule that converts near-infrared light into heat. This allows the muscles to tighten after directly exposing them to a lamp. That said, the process isn’t as simple as sticking the elastomers onto their model frog and dropping it into water.

“Getting the six muscles to work together was a major challenge,” explained Brigitte Städler, a study co-author and Aarhus University chemist. “If they don’t contract in a coordinated way, the frog won’t swim forwards. It may simply spin around.”

A lot of trial-and-error also went into concocting the elastomers themselves. In addition to contracting properly, the material needed the proper consistency to use in a 3D printer. To do this, Ryberg experimented with various molecular ingredients and molecule chain lengths to perfect the robot muscle recipe.

“In a conventional 3D printer, you typically melt a solid plastic filament. Our material is more like very thick syrup or icing that you squeeze through a piping bag when decorating a cake,” said Ryberg.

The final result is a light-powered soft robot that’s quite unique, but also not in any hurry. At its best pace, the frog swam a little over three inches in about two minutes. That may not get it to its destination quickly, but the proof-of-concept successfully offers a new way to think about robotic design, and the ways engineers can power their creations. Until then, there is always the potential for robo-frog toys.

#4728. How Non-Dairy Creamers Doubled Coffee’s Calories For Many Americans

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

By 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

The researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

The researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

Coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

However, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she said.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

“Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

More than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:

“These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” said Kirkpatrick.

She also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“I suggest that my patients try to embrace a black cup of coffee as opposed to starting the day with sugar,” Kirkpatrick said.

She suggested that certain additions, such as chicory root or cinnamon, may enhance your brew while still providing benefits. Plain milk can also provide protein and calcium without added sugar.

“Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an important factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” said Kirkpatrick.

#4727. Honda’s $2,000 electric moped is a winner. So why can’t Americans buy it?

Honda has been steadily expanding its electric motorcycle lineup, but one of its most interesting new models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine. It’s a modest little electric scooter called the Honda UC3, and with prices now dipping close to $2,000 in local markets, it’s the kind of affordable electric two-wheeler that many Americans would probably love to get their hands on.

Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.

We first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the company announced plans to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam. Designed as an electric equivalent to a 110cc gasoline-powered scooter, the UC3 is built for practical everyday transportation rather than weekend joyrides.

But don’t let its modest appearance fool you. The UC3 packs a 6 kW (8 hp) electric motor capable of reaching approximately 50 mph (80 km/h), making it more than capable of handling typical urban commuting.

Its 3.2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery provides up to 76 miles (122 km) of range under WMTC testing. Unlike Honda’s other electric scooters that use removable batteries, the UC3 has a permanently installed battery that charges directly on the bike.

There’s also a full-color TFT display, smartphone connectivity, three riding modes, reverse gear, and a generous 26-liter under-seat storage compartment.

And perhaps most importantly, it comes from Honda, a company with decades of experience building reliable, affordable motorcycles.

The UC3 originally launched in Vietnam with prices starting around 78.5 million Vietnamese dong, or roughly $3,000. However, recent reports from Vietnamese dealerships show incentives bringing prices down to around 54 million dong, equivalent to approximately $2,100.

That’s a pretty compelling price for a 50 mph (80 km/h) electric scooter from one of the world’s largest motorcycle manufacturers.

But despite its appeal, Honda hasn’t announced any plans to bring the UC3 to the United States.

In much of Southeast Asia, scooters are everyday transportation, with millions of riders using them for commuting, shopping, and practically everything else. In the US, motorcycles are much more commonly recreational vehicles, and the market for small, practical scooters is comparatively tiny.

I'm hoping scooters like this take over the world, the sooner the better. Anyone who's travelled in any cities in Asian, India, or most of Europe, there's always a constant background whine of 2-stroke scooters, day and night.

I would have thought these kinds of markets would have already transitioned to EV - in addition to the annoying sound, those 2-stroke engines spew out an order of magnitude more pollution than most ICE vehicles. I guess it's been a cost issue - this scooter should be cheap enough to take over the world.

Add in the costs of US regulatory certification, establishing parts and service support, and navigating a market where many buyers expect motorcycles to handle highway speeds, and the business case becomes considerably less attractive.

That’s unfortunate, because the UC3 looks like exactly the kind of electric two-wheeler that could make a real difference in American cities.

It’s affordable, practical, fast enough for most city streets, and backed by a manufacturer that isn’t going anywhere.

Now if only Honda would give Americans a chance to buy one.
